When someone is aggrieved, they feel that they have been treated unfairly or wrongly — and they are upset, hurt, or resentful because of it. It is a specific kind of emotional pain. Not just sadness from a bad day, but the sharp, stinging feeling of "this was done to me, and it wasn't right."

Think of it as hurt + a sense of injustice, combined.
What Makes It Different From Just Being "Upset"

Many words describe negative feelings. "Aggrieved" is special because it always involves a perceived wrong or injustice. The person doesn't just feel bad — they feel mistreated. There is always a cause: someone did something unfair, dismissive, disrespectful, or hurtful to them.

If you are sad because it rained on your picnic, you are disappointed — but not aggrieved. But if your colleague took credit for your hard work in front of your boss, and you feel hurt and resentful about that injustice, that is being aggrieved.
Does the Wrong Have to Be Real?

No — and this is an important nuance. A person can be aggrieved over a real wrong or a perceived wrong. In other words, they might genuinely have been treated unfairly, or they might only believe they were treated unfairly (even if others disagree). What defines the word is the feeling of having been wronged, not whether that feeling is objectively justified.

For example:

  • A worker who was truly denied a deserved promotion feels aggrieved. ✅ Real wrong.
  • Someone who feels their friend's honest feedback was "too harsh" might also feel aggrieved. ✅ Perceived wrong — even if the feedback was fair.

Both uses of the word are correct.
How "Aggrieved" Shows Up in a Person

When someone is aggrieved, it usually comes out in one of these ways:

In their face or body language — An aggrieved person often looks sulky, wounded, or quietly indignant. They may appear to be quietly seething or visibly hurt. You might say someone has "an aggrieved look" on their face.

In their voice or tone — They may speak in an aggrieved tone — a voice that signals they feel wronged. It might sound bitter, resentful, quietly angry, or emotionally injured.

In their behavior — They may complain, withdraw, seek an apology, demand justice, or confront the person who wronged them.

In law and formal contexts, "aggrieved" has a precise and important meaning. The aggrieved party refers to the person who has suffered a legal wrong, harm, or injury — the one who has grounds to file a complaint or take legal action. Courts often use this language.

For example: "The court ruled in favor of the aggrieved party and ordered compensation."

Here, "aggrieved" doesn't just mean emotionally upset — it means the person was legally wronged and has a legitimate claim to seek a remedy.
How It's Used in a Sentence

Here are examples across different situations so you can see the word in action:

  • "She felt aggrieved when she was left out of the meeting that directly concerned her work."
  • "He gave me an aggrieved look when I forgot to invite him."
  • "The aggrieved employees filed a formal complaint against the manager."
  • "She spoke in an aggrieved tone, clearly still hurting from the criticism."
  • "He felt deeply aggrieved by the way the situation had been handled."
  • "The aggrieved customers demanded a refund after the company broke its promises."
  • "Even after the apology, she still seemed aggrieved."

"Aggrieved" can describe feelings that range from mild to deep:

  • Mildly aggrieved: A friend forgot to text you back and you feel a little slighted.
  • Deeply aggrieved: You were falsely accused of something serious at work and feel profoundly wronged.

The word works across this whole spectrum. Context and other words around it (like "deeply," "visibly," "quietly") usually tell you how intense the feeling is.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Offended — Feeling offended is about something that violated your dignity or sensibilities (a rude comment, a tasteless joke). Aggrieved goes a step deeper — it involves a sense that something was actually done against you unfairly.

Wronged — To feel wronged is very close to aggrieved. The difference is subtle: "wronged" focuses on the act that happened to you, while "aggrieved" focuses on the emotional state resulting from that act.

Resentful — Resentment is a lingering, bitter feeling from being treated unfairly. A person who is aggrieved may become resentful over time if the wrong is never addressed.

Indignant — Indignant means angry because something is unfair or unjust. A person who is aggrieved often feels indignant, but "indignant" is more about active anger, while "aggrieved" emphasizes the emotional wound and sense of being a victim of injustice.
Aggrieved describes someone who feels emotionally hurt, resentful, or wounded because they believe they have been treated unjustly or wrongly — whether that wrong was real or only perceived.
